title: Introduction to Law
summary: Understand sources of law, courts, contracts, negligence, criminal law and legal method, with examples from common law and mixed systems.
audience: Students, paralegals, business owners and anyone new to law

lessons.title: What law is and where it comes from

body.p: Law is a system of rules that a society recognises and enforces through institutions such as courts and police. Its main purposes are to keep order, protect rights, settle disputes and guide behaviour. Law differs from morality: something can be morally wrong without being illegal, and some legal rules are simply practical, such as which side of the road to drive on.

list: Constitution: the highest law in most countries; other laws must agree with it.
Legislation (statutes or Acts): rules written by parliament or a national assembly.
Case law (precedent): earlier court decisions that later courts follow.
Custom: long-practised community rules, recognised in many African legal systems alongside statute.
Treaties and international law: agreements between states.

body.p: Two broad traditions shape most legal systems. In common law systems, such as Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya and the United Kingdom, judges follow precedent. In civil law systems, such as Spain, courts rely mainly on written codes. Many countries mix traditions, for example South Africa combines Roman-Dutch and English law with customary law.

body.tip: When you meet a legal question, always ask first: which country, and which source of law applies?

body.p: Courts apply the law to real disputes. They are arranged in a hierarchy. Lower courts, such as magistrates' courts, hear many simple cases. Higher courts hear serious cases and appeals. At the top is the supreme or constitutional court, whose decisions bind all lower courts.

The doctrine of precedent, called stare decisis, means a court should follow earlier decisions of higher courts on similar facts. This makes the law predictable and fair, because like cases are treated alike. A court may distinguish a case if its facts are materially different, and a higher court may overrule an earlier decision that it thinks was wrong.

list: Civil: a private party sues another, usually for compensation or an order. The claimant must prove the case on the balance of probabilities, meaning more likely than not.
Criminal: the state prosecutes a person for a crime. The prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt, a higher standard.
The outcome in civil cases is liability and a remedy; in criminal cases it is conviction and punishment.

body.tip: The burden of proof is always on the party who brings the case, and the standard is much higher in criminal law because liberty is at stake.

body.p: A contract is an agreement that the law will enforce. For most contracts, four elements are needed: offer, acceptance, consideration and an intention to create legal relations. Capacity and legality are also required.

list: Offer: a clear proposal on definite terms, for example to sell a phone for 50,000.
Acceptance: unconditional agreement to that offer. A reply with changed terms is a counter-offer, not an acceptance.
Consideration: something of value exchanged by each side, such as money for goods.
Intention: the parties must mean the agreement to be legally binding. Social promises between friends usually are not.
Capacity and legality: the parties must be old enough and of sound mind, and the purpose must be lawful.

body.p: If one party fails to perform without a lawful excuse, that is a breach. The usual remedy is damages, money meant to put the innocent party in the position they would have been in if the contract had been performed. Courts can sometimes order specific performance, which means doing what was promised.
Example: Ada offers to sell her laptop to Tunde for 200,000. Tunde says he will pay 180,000. That is a counter-offer, so Ada is free to refuse. If Ada then says yes, a contract is formed at 180,000.
A tort is a civil wrong that causes harm to another person, outside of a contract. The victim can claim compensation. The most common tort is negligence.

To succeed in negligence, the claimant must show three things. First, the defendant owed a duty of care, for example a driver owes a duty to other road users. Second, the defendant breached that duty by failing to act as a reasonable person would. Third, the breach caused damage that was not too remote. If any element is missing, the claim fails.

list: Duty: would a reasonable person foresee harm to someone like the claimant?
Breach: did the defendant fall below the standard of a reasonable person?
Causation: would the harm have happened but for the breach?
Damage: loss or injury that the law recognises.

body.p: Other torts include defamation (harming someone's reputation with false statements), nuisance (unreasonable interference with the use of land) and trespass. Defences include consent and contributory negligence, where the claimant's own carelessness reduces the damages. For example, a motorcyclist hit by a careless driver who was not wearing a helmet may have compensation reduced.

Criminal law defines acts the state treats as crimes and sets punishments. Most crimes have two parts: the guilty act, called actus reus, and the guilty mind, called mens rea. Both must be proved. A person who takes an identical umbrella by honest mistake lacks the intention to steal.

list: Offences against the person: murder, manslaughter, assault.
Property offences: theft, robbery, fraud, arson.
Public order and corruption offences.
Regulatory offences, where intention may not be needed.

body.p: Most constitutions and the Universal Declaration of Human Rights protect certain basic rights for accused persons. These include the presumption of innocence, the right to be told the charge, the right to a lawyer, the right to be heard by an impartial court, and protection from torture or forced confessions. Evidence obtained unlawfully may be excluded.
Defences include self-defence, duress, insanity and mistake. A defence can lead to acquittal or a reduced charge depending on the facts.

body.tip: A person is innocent until proved guilty. The accused never has to prove innocence in a typical criminal trial.

lessons.title: Reading law, legal method and ethics

body.p: Lawyers use a simple method often remembered as IRAC: Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion. First identify the legal issue. Then state the rule that applies, from a statute or case. Apply the rule to the facts, and finally give a conclusion.

Courts read statutes by their ordinary words first (the literal rule). If that leads to an absurd result, they may look at the purpose of the law (the purposive approach). Definitions sections, headings and the long title help to show what the legislature meant.

list: Confidentiality: lawyers must not reveal client information without consent or legal duty.
Conflict of interest: a lawyer must not act for two parties whose interests clash.
Duty to the court: lawyers must not mislead the court.
Competence and diligence: take only work you can do properly and on time.

body.p: Note that this course is general education. It is not legal advice, and laws differ between countries and change over time. For a real legal problem, speak to a qualified lawyer or a legal aid centre in your country.

quiz.q: Which source of law is normally the highest in a country?

options: Judges choose any rule they like
Every case must go to appeal
Courts should follow earlier decisions of higher courts on similar facts

quiz.q: What is the standard of proof in a civil case?
In a criminal case, who must prove guilt?
Ada offers to sell a laptop for 200,000. Tunde replies he will pay 180,000. What is Tunde's reply in law?
Which of these is NOT normally required for a valid contract?
options: A written deed in every case

quiz.q: What is the usual remedy for breach of contract?
options: Fine paid to the claimant's friends

quiz.q: Which is the first element of negligence?
A claimant's own carelessness reduces damages. What is this called?
What are actus reus and mens rea?
options: The guilty act and the guilty mind

quiz.q: Which is a fair trial right?
options: Trial without being told the charge
Judge who is a party to the case

quiz.q: Under the literal rule, how do courts first read a statute?
options: By guessing what the minister wanted

quiz.q: Which duty does a lawyer owe to a client?
options: To act for both sides of a dispute
